**Rebuttal (Debater B)**

Debater A's answer fails on a concrete instance. Give all 2025 people the identical weights $p_c = \frac{248}{517\,q_c}$, with 44 colors at $q_c = 32$ and 22 at $q_c = 31$. These sum to 1. Since $\sum_c (q_c - 1) = 2024 < 2025$, every assignment gives some color at least $q_{c_0}$ people, so its load is at least $\frac{248}{517} \approx 0.4797$. Any valid $C$ must therefore be at least $248/517$, and $31/66 \approx 0.4697$ is refuted.

A's step 1 correctly proves $C \ge 31/66$, but that is only a floor. Step 2 maximizes over a one-parameter family that doesn't contain my instance, and step 4's exact $31/66$ comes from the uniform distribution, which my construction beats. A's "natural family peaks at uniform" claim is therefore irrelevant to the true maximum.

A also concedes that its upper bound is unproven. So A has no argument that 31/66 is achievable against all distributions, and a rigorous counterexample against it. To keep 31/66, A must show that every weight matrix admits an assignment at load $31/66$, which its own caveat says it cannot do.

I grant that my matching upper bound, which shows identical weights are the worst case, is not yet fully proven. But the lower-bound counterexample already rules out 31/66.
